name: Mesopotamia
summary: Mesopotamia's civilizations rose and fell in succession along the Tigris and Euphrates: Sumerian city-states gave way to Sargon's Akkadian Empire, then the Sumerian revival under the Third Dynasty of Ur, Hammurabi's Babylon, the Neo-Assyrian Empire centered on Nineveh, and finally the Neo-Babylonian Empire, which fell to Cyrus the Great of Persia in 539 BC.
imageAttribution: Map by Goran tek-en, CC BY-SA 4.0, via Wikimedia Commons
imageDescription: A map of ancient Mesopotamia along the Tigris and Euphrates rivers.

events.title: Cuneiform Emerges at Uruk
events.body: The world's earliest writing system develops from clay tokens used to record grain and livestock at the city of Uruk, becoming the first script for recording language and law.
events.imageAttribution: Photo by Bjørn Christian Tørrissen, CC BY-SA 3.0, via Wikimedia Commons
events.imageDescription: A monumental Achaemenid-era cuneiform inscription of Xerxes I, carved into the cliff at Van in eastern Turkey.

events.title: Sargon Founds the Akkadian Empire
events.body: Sargon of Akkad conquers the Sumerian city-states and unites them under a single ruler, creating what many historians consider the world's first empire.
events.imageAttribution: Photo by ALFGRN, CC BY-SA 2.0, via Wikimedia Commons
events.imageDescription: Sargon of Akkad depicted on his victory stele.

events.title: Enheduanna Composes Sacred Hymns
events.body: Enheduanna, high priestess of the moon god Nanna at Ur and daughter of Sargon of Akkad, writes hymns to the goddess Inanna that scribes keep copying for centuries, making her the first author in world history known by name.
events.imageAttribution: Photo by Mefman00, CC0, via Wikimedia Commons
events.imageDescription: The alabaster Disk of Enheduanna, showing her performing a religious libation ceremony.

events.title: Gutian Invaders Topple the Akkadian Empire
events.body: Raiders from the Gutian people overrun southern Mesopotamia and end Akkadian rule, plunging the region into roughly a century of fragmented, weakened kingship before Ur-Nammu's revival.
events.imageAttribution: Photo by Osama Shukir Muhammed Amin FRCP(Glasg), CC BY-SA 4.0, via Wikimedia Commons
events.imageDescription: A votive mace head dedicated by La-arab, a Gutian king, now in the British Museum.

events.title: Ur-Nammu Founds the Third Dynasty of Ur
events.body: After centuries of Akkadian and Gutian rule, Ur-Nammu reunites southern Mesopotamia under the city of Ur and issues the Code of Ur-Nammu, the oldest law code known to survive.
events.imageAttribution: Map by Sémhur and Zunkir, CC BY-SA 3.0, via Wikimedia Commons
events.imageDescription: A map of the Third Dynasty of Ur's territorial extent under Ur-Nammu and Shulgi.

events.title: Ur-Nammu Begins the Great Ziggurat of Ur
events.body: Ur-Nammu breaks ground on a massive stepped temple platform dedicated to the moon god Nanna, a project his son Shulgi completes -- one of the best-preserved ziggurats surviving from ancient Mesopotamia.
events.imageAttribution: Photo by Tla2006, Public domain, via Wikimedia Commons
events.imageDescription: The reconstructed ziggurat of Ur, built under Ur-Nammu and Shulgi.

events.title: Elamites Sack Ur, Ending the Third Dynasty
events.body: An Elamite army captures Ur and its king Ibbi-Sin, extinguishing the Third Dynasty after two decades of territorial collapse and closing the last great flowering of Sumerian civilization.
events.imageAttribution: Photo via the Metropolitan Museum of Art, CC0, via Wikimedia Commons
events.imageDescription: A depiction of Ibbi-Sin, the last king of the Third Dynasty of Ur, enthroned.

events.title: Hammurabi's Code Carved in Stone
events.body: Babylon's king publishes 282 laws on a black diorite stele, one of the earliest surviving law codes governing an entire society.
events.imageAttribution: Photo by Mbzt, CC BY 3.0, via Wikimedia Commons
events.imageDescription: The front face of the Code of Hammurabi stele, now in the Louvre.

events.title: Hittites Sack Babylon, Ending Hammurabi's Dynasty
events.body: Hittite king Mursili I raids deep into Mesopotamia and sacks Babylon, toppling the First Babylonian Dynasty founded by Hammurabi and opening the way for the Kassites to take the throne.
events.imageAttribution: Map by MapMaster, CC BY-SA 4.0, via Wikimedia Commons
events.imageDescription: A map of Babylonia under the Kassite dynasty that succeeded Hammurabi's fallen dynasty.

events.title: The Epic of Gilgamesh Reaches Its Standard Form
events.body: Scholar-priest Sin-Leqi-Unninni compiles the definitive version of the Epic of Gilgamesh, weaving older Sumerian and Akkadian poems about the legendary king of Uruk into the work that survives today as the world's oldest known epic.
events.imageAttribution: Photo by BabelStone, CC0, via Wikimedia Commons
events.imageDescription: The Flood Tablet, the eleventh tablet of the Epic of Gilgamesh, from the Library of Ashurbanipal.

events.title: Adad-nirari II Founds the Neo-Assyrian Empire
events.body: Adad-nirari II's accession launches a newly aggressive phase of Assyrian expansion that grows, over the next three centuries, into the largest empire the world had yet seen.
events.imageAttribution: Map by Ningyou, Public domain, via Wikimedia Commons
events.imageDescription: A map of the Assyrian Empire at its territorial extent.

events.title: Sennacherib Destroys Babylon
events.body: After Babylon's king allies with Elam and Assyria's own crown prince is captured and executed, Sennacherib razes the rebellious city and diverts a canal to flood its ruins, declaring the land kingless.
events.imageAttribution: Photo by Gary Todd, CC0, via Wikimedia Commons
events.imageDescription: An Assyrian bas-relief of armed soldiers from the palace of King Sennacherib.

events.title: Esarhaddon Rebuilds Babylon
events.body: Esarhaddon reverses his father's destruction of Babylon, resettling its people and restoring the Esagila temple and Etemenanki ziggurat in a project his successors will need decades to finish.
events.imageAttribution: Photo by Osama Shukir Muhammed Amin FRCP(Glasg), CC BY-SA 4.0, via Wikimedia Commons
events.imageDescription: The Assyrian king Esarhaddon depicted on a commemorative stele from Sam'al, now in the Pergamon Museum.

events.title: Ashurbanipal Builds the Library at Nineveh
events.body: Assyrian king Ashurbanipal assembles a vast collection of cuneiform tablets at his capital, creating the ancient world's most systematic library and preserving countless Mesopotamian texts for posterity.
events.imageAttribution: Photo by KeyolTranslater, CC BY-SA 4.0, via Wikimedia Commons
events.imageDescription: A relief of King Ashurbanipal hunting lions, from his palace at Nineveh.

events.title: Nabopolassar Founds the Neo-Babylonian Empire
events.body: A former Assyrian official, Nabopolassar seizes Babylon amid Assyria's succession crisis and is crowned king, launching the revolt that destroys the Neo-Assyrian Empire within two decades.
events.imageAttribution: Map by ܥܘܡܪܐ, Public domain, via Wikimedia Commons
events.imageDescription: A map of the Neo-Babylonian Empire founded by Nabopolassar.

events.title: Nineveh Falls
events.body: A coalition of Babylonians and Medes storms the Assyrian capital, ending the Neo-Assyrian Empire's centuries of dominance over the Near East.
events.imageAttribution: Illustration by Mu-tamajo, CC BY-SA 4.0, via Wikimedia Commons
events.imageDescription: John Martin's 1829 painting The Fall of Nineveh.

events.title: Nebuchadnezzar II Rebuilds the Etemenanki Ziggurat
events.body: Nebuchadnezzar II raises Babylon's great ziggurat to a scale later Greek and biblical writers mythologize as the Tower of Babel, cementing Babylon's reputation as the ancient world's most spectacular city.
events.imageAttribution: Illustration by Jona Lendering, Public domain, via Wikimedia Commons
events.imageDescription: A reconstruction drawing of the Etemenanki ziggurat, based on Hansjörg Schmid's research.

events.title: Nebuchadnezzar II Conquers Jerusalem
events.body: After a lengthy siege, Babylonian forces breach Jerusalem's walls, destroy Solomon's Temple, and deport much of the population -- the start of the Babylonian captivity that Cyrus will later end.
events.imageAttribution: Public domain, via Wikimedia Commons
events.imageDescription: A depiction of Etemenanki, the great ziggurat of Babylon rebuilt under Nebuchadnezzar II.

events.title: Nabonidus Abandons Babylon for Tayma
events.body: Devoted to the moon god Sin over Babylon's own patron deity Marduk, King Nabonidus withdraws to the Arabian oasis of Tayma for roughly a decade, leaving his son Belshazzar as regent and alienating Babylon's priesthood.
events.imageAttribution: Photo by Osama Shukir Muhammed Amin FRCP(Glasg), CC BY-SA 4.0, via Wikimedia Commons
events.imageDescription: A relief of King Nabonidus before the crescent symbol of the moon god Sin, to whom he was devoted.

events.title: Cyrus the Great Takes Babylon
events.body: Cyrus of Persia captures Babylon without a major battle, ending the Neo-Babylonian Empire and folding Mesopotamia into the Achaemenid Empire.
events.imageAttribution: Mezzotint by J. Martin (1831), CC BY 4.0, via Wikimedia Commons / Wellcome Collection
events.imageDescription: J. Martin's 1831 mezzotint depicting Cyrus the Great's conquest of Babylon.
